utterances.text: You, who had a Croatian mother and who have many friends who are Croats, you say you supported the Dinamo club from Zagreb in soccer, and you were friendly with the people. You were monitoring. And yet you agreed to monitor them, to spy on them. Can you tell us what your motivation was for doing something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, it was pragmatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it boiled down to money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Money and everything that money brings with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well then. Can you tell me what you discovered? Did the -- were the priest Kljajic and Coban, agents of foreign intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted reports on their activities, and, of course, I was unable to judge whether they were or were not foreign agents. Robert Coban did receive certain financial assistance, some of it from the US embassy, from Mr. Lee to be specific, who in those years was a representative of the embassy in Belgrade and who visited Marko Kljajic also. As I have already said, they asked me to be present at Marko Kljajic's when certain people visited him. And as for Reverend Beslic, Milovan Popivoda told me that they had reliable information that he was in the employ of the Croatian service for the protection of the constitutional order and that he was meeting him in Osijek, that he met him during one of his trips there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned several persons whom you talked to, monitored at the time, and these talks were mostly held in Novi Sad. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Novi Sad, and on several occasions I travelled with Reverend Marko Kljajic to Zagreb where I met some people who Milovan Popivoda told me were of interest to the intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And yesterday, you listed four men who had conversations in Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anything happen to any of these people? Were they arrested as foreign agents? Did anything happen to them? To any of the four you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told to pay attention to the contacts of Marko Kljajic with these people, Melvinger, Kraljevic and others. And if you ask whether anything happened to any of them, yes. Niko Kraljevic, the priest, was attacked on several occasions in Hrtkovci in mid-1992. And Marko Kljajic testified to this in his book, "How My People Died."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that. Now, tell me, please, and answer my question directly, as you say that your boss was in charge of liquidations, were you ever tasked with some liquidations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to that is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't liquidate anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as I can see from what you just said a moment ago, you did organise the mistreatment of an elderly woman. That is the mother of this Catholic priest who was a close friend of yours, Marko Kljajic. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in that but I didn't organise it. I receive the order from Milovan Popivoda, the chief of the Novi Sad DB centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does he know that you are behind this attack on his mother, you as his close friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't know up until this moment, but I assume yesterday if he is following the trial, I assume that he understood who is in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me the names of those refugees who, as you say -- as you say in your statement how she attacked them and they had to deal with her and then they escaped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that she retaliated, not that she attacked. They didn't expect any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't you think that this was a very strange attack on an old lady as you explain it here, as you say they managed to overpower her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. There was a conflict. There was a clash. The woman was resilient. She responded regardless of the fact that she's old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You described this event. How did it actually happen? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has really covered this, Mr. Milosevic. There seems little point going over it again. He's covered it in his evidence in chief. Now, your time is limited, and there may be other things you want to cover in his evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to dwell a little bit on this topic, Mr. May. Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just briefly tell us how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in this way: They rang her doorbell, then -- however, there was always a bar near the door, which the lady who is deceased now, which the deceased Kata Kljajic used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it seem to you that you're minimising this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not minimising this event. I'm telling it the way it happened. Of course those two did not expect such a reaction, those two refugees, one of whom as far as I can recall was called Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. May I remind you how this criminal act was committed? I'm not going to quote any newspapers. I will read from Marko Kljajic's book which you mentioned. This is on page 103 of the book. He writes: "The parish house in Petro Varadin was attacked in broad daylight on the 6th of January at the end of the holidays. Two young men with iron poles broke into the parish house and seriously wounded Kata Kljajic, a woman in her late 60s. They also beat up the neighbour who later came to the aid of the old lady." This is why I'm asking you. Why are you minimising this event? You said that they rang the doorbell, she opened the door and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness should be able to answer first of all. You've heard the account, Witness C-048, which has been read out -- which has been read - just a moment - which has been read out. You weren't, of course, present, nor was the author, I suspect. Now, does that accord, as far as you know, with what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the story in the book is somewhat exaggerated. Marko Kljajic liked to exaggerate a little bit, particularly because the money for the publication of this book was received from the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Croatia. It's not true that she was beaten by iron bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They did not break down the door with iron bars and they did not beat her with iron rods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say about the door but I saw her a couple of days later and I would have surely noticed if she had sustained injuries inflicted by rods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you cannot say anything about the door, why did you then say that they rang the doorbell and opened it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Our time is limited. We've been over this incident. The witness has described it. Now, move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Marko Kljajic's report I have a report here, a medical report. It's a photocopy, it's not very legible, but it's possible to get the book itself. So do you know who are these friends of yours who broke down the parish house door, the parish house door in Petro Varadin with rods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not any friends of mine. I explained to the Honourable Court my role in this incident. It was up to me to tell Milan Popivoda [sic] when Marko Kljajic is not at home, to tell him when he would be absent for a longer time. When I say "longer time," I mean more than a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that book -- from -- from the -- book -- in the book it says there was a man who lived opposite the street, in a house across the street, and he came and -- because the man heard the noise, he came to the house and he rescued her. And then in the book it says they managed to overcome her because -- they didn't manage to overcome her. She continued to fight. But in the book it says that they managed to beat up this man too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this. This is one incident, a relatively small one, although important obviously for those involved and serious enough at the time. But compared with the amount of evidence this witness has given, you are wasting the time of the Tribunal. We've heard what you've put. Now, either you move on to something else or this examination is brought to an end. It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that one of those attackers was Mirko Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to consider stopping this. You have been told to move on. You have declined to do so. We're going to consider whether this whole cross-examination doesn't come to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I have very important questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. I suspect you're just about to announce are decision, but before you do, may I make one contribution to the concerns that the Chamber has expressed about Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 19756 to 19764.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: knowing the pattern of the Trial Chamber in allowing an equal amount of time for cross-examination to examination-in-chief takes time with what is irrelevant in order to justify after the event, as it were, the limited time he might spend on the really material issues. Here, the meetings of which evidence has been given by this witness are topics that it really is important that the accused should deal with, and indeed under the Rules of the Tribunal could almost be compelled to deal with if he is to cross-examine at all, and obviously we would be very anxious that he should by one means or another bring his attention to those topics and put his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You've got one hour and ten minutes left. During that time, if you challenge any form of the conversation which you had, which took place in your presence and you were involved in, if you don't challenge that, we will except the account which the witness gives as accurate. You must understand that. So if you're challenging that, you must do so or it will be accepted as accurate. Now, you can tell us, if there is, what the relevance of the minute detail of this particular attack on Mr. Kljajic's mother is. What is the relevance of the detail as to whether iron poles were used or what happened? What's the relevance of that? And if it's relevant, we'll consider allowing you to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I am disputing not only this witness's statement but this witness as a whole. The relevance lies in the fact that the witness speaking about this incident which really was an individual incident said that the press wrote about it in order to frighten other Croats, and that is why I'm putting to him the question whether our press wrote about it in order to frighten other Croats or the press wrote about it in order to condemn this crime that happened. Did it write about it in order to promote such violence or to the contrary, to condemn this crime so that it would not be repeated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must ask the witness to clarify his statement. If the reports that you say were given were intended to frighten the Croats, if you say that was the reason, why do you say so? What is your reason for saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I say that on the basis of the fact that in December 1992, Milovan Popivoda told me that Marko Kljajic, the priest, should be pressed so that he would move out of Vojvodina. And the reason for that was that Reverend Marko Kljajic would dissuade his parishioners from moving out to Croatia. He persuaded them to stay on their hearths and reserve their ethnic identity. In my statement, regarding that event, I mentioned it, but what I basically wanted to say was that the political objective of that event was for the remaining Croats in Vojvodina to start to think in the following way: If we see what they're doing to the reverend, what are they going to do to us? Reverend Marko Kljajic told me after that, "I am not going to move out, even if they kill me on our own hearth." So the details on which the accused is insisting, such as the iron bars or whatever, are not important. The political nature of that -- of the event is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I am asking you, did the press write about if in such a way as to condemn this event, expressing general condemnation of that event? Did you look at the press from that time? Did the press condemn this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course officially it did condemn this act, but the political message behind that was very clear. What good is it to some victim if the perpetrators will be sentenced if they get killed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You're saying the press used to do that to frighten Croats. If the press condemned that, how can you say that something else was behind that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was to inform the public what happened to the reverend and so that the other parishioners would start thinking along the lines of: If this is what they're doing to the reverend, what are they going to do to us? It doesn't matter to a person if they're killed later what will happen later, whether this act would be condemned or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: What, according to you, would happen if the press did not write about an event? What would have happened if the press had ignored such an event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such attacks. You know that very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't know that very well. Quite the opposite. We looked after all of the citizens in Serbia, Muslims, Croats, and members of all ethnicities, so that is precisely why I don't know about that. I don't know that there was any violence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am keeping to your instructions. I do not wish to enter into discussion with the accused here. As far as the question regarding the writing of the press, I said that there were political objectives, and I replied to that and if something is unclear, then I will reply to that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please tell me, did the press condemn this event or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, formally they did. Nobody was gleeful about it in the press. They did condemn it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: There is no point in continuing on along these lines with this question any more. Could you please tell us about this so-called diary of yours? Do you have a diary or do you not have a diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it at the moment. Nobody asked for it. The investigators, when they visited me at my house were able to see it. I don't have it here. Only later after I came to a certain place was I asked about this diary. I'm speaking generally, in general terms like this so we do not have to move into a private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: That is not important. I do not wish to move into a private session. But you do not have a diary, is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I don't have it now. I didn't think I would need it here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Would you be able to obtain it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that we already talked about this during private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Does that mean that your diary has been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So you do not have a diary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And these notes allegedly which are extracts from your diary, you copied from that diary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part was copied, and a part were just reminders to me about certain things so that I would not forget to talk about them, and this is obvious when you look at the notes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't know whether there is any need to move into private session, but in the accompanying document to these alleged notes, it says that the witness provided the following explanation: "[In English] Rewrote from my original diary when I was preparing myself for" -- [No Interpretation] -- "[In English] I left the original ..." [Interpretation] And so on. I'm not going to identify this now. And he says that the diary was destroyed after his departure but that these notes can be of use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So you don't have any proof that you had a diary at all from which you would have been able to make these notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary was on the table at my house in front of the investigators on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But the investigators did not instruct you that you needed to bring the diary with you? They didn't give you any specific instructions about this document that you had? They didn't tell you that you need to bring the diary with you when you come to The Hague, is that what your sea saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me I had to bring the diary with me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Nobody told you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I agree with what you have just said now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You did not have a diary at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not say that. The accused, as usual, is lying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think it's quite the opposite. It is incredible that somebody's proving something with something that they allegedly copied from something and then say that they had destroyed the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's all by way of comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you accept documents here which are in fact not documents. That's up to you and it's your method. I'm not going to involve myself in that. But it's quite clear that he doesn't have the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is another comment. We've heard what the witness said. We'll have to make our minds up about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm quite prepared to call the investigator who was at the witness's house to say whether there was indeed a diary apparent to him existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have been the Bible or anything else, the Holy Scriptures on the book -- on the table or anything else. Why would somebody destroy a piece of evidence which they rely on? But let's go on to the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 5 of your statement, you say that many influential people often visited the casino, and among them you mention my name too. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Now, tell me this. When was it that I visited the casino?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first weeks of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And you made a note of that in your diary, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. Let me now ask you something quite specific. When one keeps a diary, generally speaking, that in itself implies dates. So a diary is kept on a daily basis usually, day by day. So what date was I there then in your casino? What does it say about that in your diary? What was the date you had this entry in when you say I visited this casino. Do you have a date? If you say it's a diary you must have dates and entries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an official diary. It was my own private diary, Your Honours, which I would put entries in from time to time. It's true that people sometimes stick to dates, but they're usually adolescents who have a lot of time to do a lot of writing in their diaries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, many famous people throughout the world who keep diaries write dates in their diaries and that's why the book is called a diary in the first place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They write official diaries. I didn't say it was an official diary. It was my private diary. Of course I did have official records too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So you don't have any date? That's right, isn't it, no dates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we have located the time, pinpointed the time close enough.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, assume that you don't know that I never in my life visited a casino of any kind either in my own country or abroad.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the accused was in the casino itself. I said that he was on the premises of MP Royal, which has a casino, cafeteria, and restaurant within its complex. I didn't say that you were in the casino and least of all did I say that you were there to gamble.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. So I was in the cafeteria, was I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The cafeteria or restaurant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. Cafeteria or restaurant. Now, you also say that a meeting was held there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Then you go on to say Vucelic, Kertes, Stanisic, Popivoda, you mention all these names. Kekovic, Pankov, and yourself. Is that right? Have I omitted anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vesko Vukotic. You omitted Vesko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: What did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vesko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Right. Vesko Vukotic as well. So I had a meeting with Vesko Vukotic as well, did I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was sitting there. I didn't say you had a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just let me find my notes about this matter and what you said yesterday. Right. Here I have it. You say that I came from the provincial board of the Socialist Party of Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Socialist Party of Serbia, the provincial board of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Right. The provincial board of the Socialist Party of Serbia and Vojvodina. Very well. Now, do you know what my -- what the position I held was in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Republic of Serbia. And you were the party chief. Whether that was your official title or whether it was frozen at that time, but any way, you were the number one man in the party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But I was the president of the republic at all events; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Fine. Now, tell me this: As you were a citizen of Novi Sad at the time generally speaking, I don't mean that particular day, date, week month, or whatever, but generally speaking, did you ever happen to see what it's like when the president of the republic arrives? Not to the town, any town, but to the town of Novi Sad, what does it generally look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw several of your arrivals in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you happen to note that there was always several thousand citizens out in the streets to greet me; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not always. When it was a classical working visit, then there weren't. But when the people were brought in from the other settlements, then there were people there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. I don't remember at any time when they weren't out in the streets, but there were so many inhabitants of Novi Sad I needn't go into that question with you. Do you know that when the -- from the time the doors of the car are open up until the time when I return to the car there is always a large number of journalists, reporters, cameramen, photographers, and so on which record my arrival, my stay, and my departure from the minute I set foot on the pavement from my car? It is a political event, the whole of my stay until I get into the car again and drive off to Belgrade. Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what every working visit of yours looked like to any town or party organisation in the country. I describe what this particular event looked like and your arrival at the Royal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. C-048, I don't want -- let's not tire ourselves with all these stories of yours and fabrications. In March 1993, I was not in Novi Sad at all, not even in the provincial board of the Socialist Party. I was never there then. According to well-checked-out information by my associates, they looked through my agendas and in March I was not in Novi Sad at all. I was in October and November during the election campaign later on. But all this is something you have fabricated. You just thought it up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not thought anything up. It's the truth and there are workers who can confirm this, employees who can bear it out. And I sincerely hope that individuals who were present at the meeting, that they will remember very well. When prodded, they will remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I assume that the directing done by the opposite side there, this is part of their job, just as it is to prove that today is Friday, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question? What's the question? Are you suggesting this is fabricated, this evidence, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, in March 1993, Mr. May, I was not in Novi Sad at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Witness, can you imagine that the president of the republic arrives to a political event of any kind, to the headquarters of the Socialist Party of Vojvodina or Serbia for Vojvodina, rather, and that he is able to go unnoticed with a few of his associates and go to no more, nor less than a casino? Don't you assume that there would not be a single newspaper in Yugoslavia which would not bring this news and say President Milosevic went to a casino, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is not a question for the witness. This is by way of comment. He says that you were there, and he reports your conversation. Now, if you've got some questions about it, more questions, you can put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You even go so far as to claim that I came from the provincial board together with Stanisic, Popivoda, Kekovic, and all the rest; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, of this list and I've made a note of it, a note of the names as you claim, that Stanisic was there, Popivoda and Kekovic, they are members of the DB; right? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marko Kekovic was director of Television Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Just Stanisic and Popivoda were DB men then, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Milan Popivoda [sic] to be specific, not to mix him up with Milutin.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, I can't mix them up because I don't know either of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know them very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. You say that and that's why you're testifying here. But do you know, for example, that never at any party meetings of any kind did Jovica Stanisic attend? He never attended any party meetings. What did he have to do at a party meeting at all to which I had allegedly come in Novi Sad? You construed that. You fabricated it all, that too. And then you say allegedly that he came with me to your casino from that party meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is why the witness is lying, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but move on. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, to move on, you go on to quote my words, what I said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Then you go on to say that I just said subtly, that I was -- they were to be subtle; right? I wrote down the word "subtle."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This isn't anything funny to me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, it is funny to me, Mr. C-048, because I never use that word in my vocabulary. And if I was to use something similar, I'd use a Serbian word. You have underestimated the differences in the level of education between the two of us. And I assume also the difference in the Serbian language and all its diversity that I use when the person told you to write down that word that I did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question is this: Did the accused use the word "subtle"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't see why this shouldn't be a Serbian word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. How -- perhaps you could just -- this is one matter I want to clarify. How were you able, C-048, to remember this conversation? You say you made your entry two or three days later. Were you present in the room all the time? How -- and if not, how were you able to remember what was said and report it as it were word-for-word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I was present in that room. My role and function was the kind I have already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So from the aspects of fact, the factual situation, I challenge that wholly. I was never in Novi Sad. But let's look at the contents and substance. Doesn't it seem to you to be amazing, Mr. C-048, as you say that I allegedly on the occasion went on to explain some sort of Greater Serbia plan, that's what you say, in the spring of 1993. Is that what you say; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although the official beginning of spring is March.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right then. Now, do you know that that was precisely when the Vance-Owen Plan was topical and running?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course you held official negotiations with the international community behind their backs, behind the backs of the international community something quite different was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. When you say that I drove for the Vance-Owen Plan to be adopted, that I at the same time made plans for a Greater Serbia, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stated here the sentences I heard uttered from the conversation. Now, what the accused had in his mind at the time I'm not is a psychiatrist to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. C-048, you never heard a conversation of that kind at all. You couldn't have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear the conversation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: It never took place, so you couldn't have heard it. And as to the direction by the other side, it's difficult to bear out. You seem to have forgotten that I was president of the republic, and therefore, nothing could have been remained a secret or confidential, anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's no secret. Many citizens of Novi Sad know that you were in the provincial board and the casino. Canak [phoen] remembers that. I don't say he was there, but he remembers, and so do other honourable citizens.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You have an excellent witness here, quite excellent. It seems you have mixed up some other things too, but there's no sense in us discussing nonsensical things of this kind. You said that in 1993, for example, it was allegedly Kertes who explained that he was having problems with communicating with Babic, whereas Hadzic was a good man, good guy. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke about the problems he was having in communicating with him up until then, and he mentioned the previous period, the events in the previous period. And you know about those events too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So Babic is bad and Hadzic is good. That's what Kertes told you, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why a comment? I have made a note of it. I have made a note of the fact that Kertes said this was in 1993 and that he had communication problems with Babic, whereas Hadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Not good and bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not good and bad. But what's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, my question, for example, is this: Did you, Mr. C-048, mix up Vance's plan and the Vance-Owen Plan, and do you know the difference at all between the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not here to speak about the differences between the Vance Plan and the Vance-Owen Plan. In this specific case, I heard Kertes say that Goran Hadzic was a good guy, that he listened, obedient, because the other one did not wish to be obedient. So they had a lot of problems to get him away from the position he was in and then prevail upon him to sign the plan. Mr. Kertes, in that context, comparing those two individuals, said that Goran Hadzic was a former warehouse clerk but was much better because he didn't meddle in other people's affairs, and he was obedient and listened to instructions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you're a partner to discuss the differences between the two plans. That's quite certain. But do you happen to recall a notorious fact, and that is that the Vance Plan in 1991 and 1992 related to the areas under UN protection in Croatia and that the Vance-Owen Plan related to Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know that at least?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What has that got to do with the witness? All the witness can say is what he heard, and that's what he's done. Now, whether we accept it or not, that's a matter for us. The intricacies of the plan are not for the witness to talk about. Maybe we'll have to consider them. No. He can only say what he heard. Now, let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the point is precisely in that he could not have heard it, because the people he worked with knew the difference and could not have made a mistake of that kind. The only person that could have made the mistake was somebody who knew nothing about either plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can make the point. You can make the comment to us when you come to address us on this witness's evidence, but there's no point asking him about these intricacies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm precisely explaining that there is a point to, because the collocutors did know the difference. It is the witness who mixed up. The collocutors could not have mixed it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What do you mean by the collocutors? What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, his collocutors were high-ranking officials of the Socialist party. And Mihalj Kertes, a state official, who would certainly not mix up the Vance Plan and the Vance-Owen Plan as the witness did. Therefore, I'm taking this as proof and evidence that this is not true and correct, that he could have told him something of that kind, but that he construed it all and fabricated it himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made the point as you've done several times over to us when you address us about it. What he said, what the witness can only answer is this: What's said is that you have made a mistake, either deliberately in reporting this conversation, you've lied about it or you've made a mistake about it. Do you follow? That's what the accused is putting. Now, is that so or not? What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the conversation did take place. Whether Mihalj Kertes said the Vance or the Vance Plan, I consider that to be completely irrelevant. The point of the conversation was to indicate Goran Hadzic's abeyance and the disobedience of Milan Babic. As for Mihalj Kertes, I don't remember that he held any state function at the time let alone participation in negotiations with the international community. In May or whatever, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's time to adjourn, in fact. Before we do let me deal with one administrative matter while it's in the Trial Chamber's mind, and that is a change in our sittings for the end of this month. We are going to now sit on the 26th and 27th of May but take the break, the health or the rest break, on the 30th of May, Friday the 30th of May and Monday the 2nd of June. We will also sit on Friday, the 6th of June. I hope that won't lead to inconvenience. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me please, Mr. May, how much time have I got left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me look. 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on for the sake of efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. C-048, do you know who Dragan Perac is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an employee of the security working in the casino from the end of 1995, and he was one of the leading people in Vojislav Seselj's radical party in Novi Sad and his nickname was Pera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He didn't work there throughout this period but from the end of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Can he confirm what you say as to who visited the casino and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have a break between question and answer, please, because the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters missed some of the dates that the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I asked you, can he confirm what you say about who visited the casino and whether it was these people who came who attended the meetings and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person named Dragan Perac can testify only to events from the end of 1995 when he became an employee of MP Royal. Whether he will agree to do so as he's one of the leaders of the Serbian Radical Party in Novi Sad and what he will say, I don't know. But I can tell you from when he was employed there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Have you heard of the companies Luka Di Konte and Yason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luka Di Konte, Dejan was the owner. He was an invalid. And as to Optika, it was Yason, Y-A-S-O-N, who was the owner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, I have it in Serbian so I didn't know what the English spelling was. You know about these two companies, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The second company was an optician shop selling glasses.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Is it true you visited these companies, racketeering there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a lie. A big lie.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well. Were you ever in prison in Zrenjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What the witness said, I think, was that others would corroborate other than others will, but we can clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: A little while ago in connection with my challenging what you said about this meeting you mentioned, you said that some other participants at this meeting will be able to corroborate your testimony and testify about this. Does this mean that you know what other people are going to come here and testify falsely against me, thus doing their dirty laundry? Is there some organisation where this is known?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the accused is asking me something I cannot answer. I said only what I know. I know that many criminals have their memories restored only when they end up in prison. So Milorad Vucelic and other people will probably recall some facts after spending some time in prison. But, Your Honours, I have had no other contacts with the Prosecution apart from my statements, and they only asked me for the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Milosevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: -- What you meant. You said at one point that Vukotic, your employer, criticised my policy as a policy of mass repression. Did this refer to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And that he explained to you that it was much more efficient to achieve goals by individual murders.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More efficient, and it didn't cause problems with the international community.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So he told you this in his criticism of me engaging in mass repression rather than individual liquidations. What kind of mass repressions were we engaging in in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no democratic institutions for the Kosovo Albanians. Police force was used on a large scale. The demonstrations of 1990 were put down, blood was spilled, and Mr. Kadriu was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You ascribe this to the service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ascribe this to the policy of which you were the leader. He emphasised to me the methods, the differences in the methods used previously and the methods used by the government which was headed by you. And this especially referred to the period beginning in mid-1995. And you know that since the end of 1997, since Djukanovic split from Bulatovic, he criticised your policy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, we have no time to go into topics connected with Montenegro. But you said that these men that you mentioned who all belonged to political and security structures - I noted this down yesterday - had a close relationship with me until around 1995 and that after that they complained that my wife was hindering their actions. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, to clarify this, because my wife had no personal relations with them, did this hindering imply what she was stating and writing in public throughout all this time against inter-ethnic conflicts, against the rejection of peace plans, against the war? Is this what you meant by hindering?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not feel called upon to comment on the articles his wife wrote in the newspapers, but Milorad Vucelic and Milan Popivoda [sic] told me that the wife of Slobodan Milosevic was acting against them. And this was a classical internecine struggle for power. And the director for radio and television Serbia said the accused's wife was responsible for the replacement. His name was Vucetic. Milan Vucetic. He said that your wife was exerting pressure on the way he was editing the news programmes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, you said that he was replaced for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what was presented in public, but he was replaced for financial misconduct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Do you know that my wife had no contacts with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know she didn't like him. That was quite clear, and he told me that on several occasions. She didn't like him or any other member of that lobby. But I don't feel called upon to comment on this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, you were a student. You probably read the newspapers. My wife published several books. I assume that you had occasion to familiarise yourself with what I'm talking about. And everything she said ran counter to the behaviour of the people with whom you were associating.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that Milorad Vucelic said the Dayton Accords signified capitulation and not an agreement, and they criticised you not for waging a Greater Serbian policy but because you were not successful in implementing it to the end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So that was the policy I conducted, but I didn't carry it through to the end.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They criticised especially you, Zivko Soklovacki in the same context. He was a local functionary, and he counted Montenegrins in positions in the magazine Duga in August 1995, an interview with Soklovacki appeared.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, now we are diverging from the main topic and I'm not interested in this interview. You said that in a conversation with Popivoda in 1996, in June or July, you asked him whether we would give Eastern Slavonia to the Croats, whether we would surrender it to them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation was in July 1996, and the context was dislocating the state security centres from eastern Croatia to Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So you said, "well, we're not going to leave that area that the Croats, are we?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And he said, no, that he was leaving some men of his there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was leaving an operative network that would function in a different manner, and he explained how, through infiltrating the transitional administration of the UN, especially the police and other services, plus classical intelligence networks such as every police has, ending in receptionists, waiters, taxi drivers, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well. What you said about receptionists and taxi drivers, let's not go into that. But do you know that in July 1996, the authorities of Eastern Slavonia and those in Zagreb had long ago signed an agreement on peaceful reintegration and that the international administration was already in place there and that the transitional period was already under way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was signed in November 1995. It began to be implemented on the 15th of January, 1996, and the deadline was one year plus one year. That is two years. And of course a certain period of time is needed in order to implement an agreement. And transferring the security of Serbia was -- from there was completed in June 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well. But there is no doubt that implementation of the agreement started six months before you had this conversation. So there was no doubt that Eastern Slavonia was to be reintegrated into Croatia and that under this agreement the Serbian population of Eastern Slavonia had some special rights. They had the right to participate in the government and so on. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: How then was it possible for you to ask him what you allegedly asked him? We're not going to surrender Eastern Slavonia to the Croats. Six months after the beginning of the implementation of the agreement on reintegration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My question referred to the intelligence contacts, because he was talking about the dislocation of the state security centres. My question to Milan Popivoda [sic] meant we're not going to give them intelligence control over these areas. I wasn't referring to military control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So you were speaking about intelligence control. I see. Well, in relation to the Republic of Serbian Krajina and so on, you say that this was occupied territory. So how is it possible, since you know about the accords that were reached which included the rights of the Serbs in that area, how could you consider that they occupied the territory on which they live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can justify my position that this was occupied territory of the Republic of Croatia because in late 1991, a Serbian aggression took place against the territory in which the Serbian police took part along with local rebel Serbs, many of whom were misled by false promises made by the Serbian authorities, although the Croatian democratic government guaranteed all their ethnic and civil rights. Your Honour, let me continue. When I say "occupation," according to the dictionary definition, occupation means that the currency use was the dinar. This was Serbian currency. Serbian telephone extensions were used. Traffic between Eastern Slavonia and Serbia took place as if it was a single country. There was no border control. That's why I used the word "occupation," although officially it was called the UNPA zone because the resolution was passed in a period where the SFRY still existed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In 1992 these were UN protected zones and there was probably a reason for that I assume, but there's no need to go into that with you in relation to your testimony. Since we have to speed up, let's move on. Yesterday during your testimony you said that the state security, as a form of special warfare against Croatia, infiltrated onto Croatian territory large amounts of narcotics, heroin, and engaged in monstrous activity which shocked you, as you said. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. And I explained what I heard from whom and when. I explained how I know this, and I talked about evidence of 600 kilogrammes of heroin in a safe belonging to the state security.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, all I wanted to establish was that you were shocked by this, and you mentioned this yesterday, and there is no doubt about it. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well. Then please explain to me, because were this true it really would be monstrous and would be really shocking. How is it possible that this important fact which shocked you so much is something that you never even mentioned in the statement that you made prior to your testimony and that you recalled it only yesterday and thought of explaining it only yesterday, this special form of warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't just yesterday that I remembered this. I the investigators about this I left Serbia. And the reason I didn't mention it before was that certain people were, unfortunately, still at large then. Now they are where they belong. And the reasons I didn't speak about this on the territory of the Republic of Serbia was for my own security, because this is something for which one can be killed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You could have said everything. But you did not say anything. You were not able to say anything about this issue with the drugs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it's the most terrible thing that I have ever heard. And because of that fact, I believe that I was under the greatest danger. I specifically said what I heard and from whom I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The reference to drugs may only have been in the version of the summary served on Monday. In fact, it had been raised with those proofing this witness throughout last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wasn't in the original statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It wasn't in the original statement. It wasn't in the earlier version of the proofing notes that the accused received, and in fact it had been raised with those assisting me throughout the previous week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Did I write down correctly, Mr. C-048, the following: The criminals which you mentioned during your testimony are Vukotic, Asanin, a certain Batko, I didn't remember his name, then Draskovic, Sobot? Did you mention anyone else of the criminals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Arkan.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your former associates are financial criminals, but if you're thinking of convicted persons, then mainly that would be the ones that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So, I'm talking about the criminals whom you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: What links do I have with any of those criminals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I'm competent to answer those questions. I explained the other facts and the circumstances. If the Trial Chamber thinks that I need to explain that, I can do that and I can briefly answer this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Unless the accused has a specific question about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Any kind of my relationship with any of those criminals whom you mentioned or with any criminal that you had ever heard about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early March 1993, I personally, at the meeting where you yourself were present, also Mr. Vesko Vukotic was present, and also through the public media and according to what Vucelic said, Raznjatovic stood three rows behind you during Badza's funeral, which I doubt that he would be able to do had he not enjoyed such trust from you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, I doubt that that would mean anything. Zeljko Raznjatovic, I saw only once in my life when he was a deputy in the national assembly, and that was an occasion when I saw all the other deputies in the hall of the national assembly. But I'm asking you do you have any knowledge of any of my contacts with any of those criminals that you have mentioned? For example, I don't even know what this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: -- Man looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's referred to the meeting in early March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could you please tell me something about this drug Mafia that operated in Belgrade and Zagreb? Does that mean that the Belgrade and the Croatian services cooperated or that the Belgrade service cooperated with the Croatian Mafia? Explain to us what this is. How was this possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain. According to what Darko Asanin and Milan Popivoda [sic] told me, Jovica Stanisic conceived the idea of getting large quantities of heroin into Croatia. This task was given to Darko Asanin who then organised the distribution through the checkpoint at Orasje. Of course --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Where is Orasje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is Orasje?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes in the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. So that we can clarify that for those who are listening to this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And Orasje was in the hands of the Croats as far as I know. At the moment it's part of the Croatian part of the Bosniak-Croatian federation. How it changed hands during the war I'm not able to specify. I said through the checkpoint in Orasje the drugs enter the Republic of Croatia. The person who did that was Zeljko Sobot who later was a victim of the Serbian and Albanian Mafia conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So did this Sobot belong to the Serbian or to the Albanian drug Mafia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he belonged to the Serbian drug Mafia but he was killed in a conflict between the Albanian and Serbian Mafia in Croatia. There were some other people who were involved in that from the intelligence and criminal milieu with whom I had intense relations with during my time in Zagreb during the NATO bombardment of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And what were you doing with the chief of this intelligence service in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Croatia football team.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he was a person that the newspapers wrote about. Our contacts were exclusively relating to sports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So it arises from this that neither the Belgrade nor the Zagreb police prosecuted any drug transactions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did prosecute that, but it is well known that specific proof is required for that. A certain group was processed only in late 1999 in this regard, out of whom nine -- out of the nine members, six of them were of Serbian ethnicity and they were found to have connections with the Serbian Security Service. One of them was Zeljko Sobot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And he is a Serb or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And criminals, particularly the DRUG Mafia, as far as I can judge, don't have any religion or any citizenship. They only have money, and that is their only faith.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that. It is true they had financial motives, but it is also true that this was the idea of Jovica Stanisic with the idea of conducting special warfare, weakening morale, and also in order to stimulate other kinds of crimes which are prompted by the drug Mafia when the majority of the territory was under occupation and half of it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: How do you get the idea at all that this originated from Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Popivoda [sic] told me this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So he was so powerful that he could infiltrate drugs into a neighbouring state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He engaged criminals to do that and you said yourself that there is no faith or ethnicity in this regard, that money is the only guide or motive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Out of all of those that participated in these narcotics transactions, you say that Sobot was killed, Asanin was killed. Are there any of them alive who would know anything about that except you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the criminal milieu, it is quite normal for them to get killed and have a short life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Is there anyone alive who could testify about this? You're talking about only the things that you have heard about, about dead people or from dead people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Popivoda [sic] is alive today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Popivoda is still working in the state security service.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's working at an institute in Belgrade and he's waiting to retire. Mr. Veselin Vukotic is also alive. He's on the run but he's alive.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes. You talked about the Special Operations Unit. Do you know that this unit was formed in early 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was formed in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I interrupt for one second while we have a passage on the screen. At line 13: 09: 30. I I've been taken to task for not raising references in the transcript to Milan Popivoda [sic]. I think you'll find from the witness that it's not Milan Popivoda [sic] as it appears on the screen but a different name, Milovan, and there is some lack of clarity in the way the words spoken have been recorded. It apparently happened on several occasions earlier in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right? It's Milovan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is Milovan Popivoda, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Let us clarify when we're talking about Popivoda. I understood that you are not accusing him of participating in the -- in drug trafficking.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said what he told me. I'm not saying that he did it. I'm just bringing out facts here and information that I heard from other people. This is what I'm doing. I don't believe that it is up to me to accuse anyone of anything. I'm here in the function of a witness and in no other function.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: What you claim now is what you heard from Popivoda, who did not participate in that himself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And from people such as Darko Asanin who did personally participate in that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, he's dead so he cannot participate in that. You mentioned Bubanj Potok. Bubanj Potok is a regular military training centre. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So, volunteers who joined the JNA were able to go to Bubanj Potok. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never went to Bubanj Potok in the autumn of 1991 so that I would be able to answer such a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned some paramilitary formations, and you mentioned Mirko Jovic, Bokan. I don't know who else. White Eagles and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. And I forgot to say that in early 1992, in the place of Bacin they committed the murder of 45 elderly persons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Do you know that all of those paramilitary formations that you mentioned belonged to the opposition parties in Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovic had a completely peripheral opposition party, and as far as Bokan is concerned, I'm not aware that he had any kind of party. Maybe a tiny party. They didn't even have deputies in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You talked about the lobby from Backa Palanka.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And you mentioned Kertes, Pankov, Stanisic, Vucelic, Kekovic, Popivoda, Frenki, Brana Crncevic. What I'm asking you, does Brana Crncevic have anything to do, Brana Crncevic, an author, have anything to do with Backa Palanka? He's not from Backa Palanka. He's not a criminal. He's not I don't know what else which you could here attribute to him. What does Vucelic have anything to do or Kekovic or Popivoda, neither of whom are from Backa Palanka or Franko Simatovic who is not from Backa Palanka either. What kind of Backa Palanka lobby is this? But let's start from Brana Crncevic. Do you know that Brana Crncevic is a writer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also a deputy of the SPS and was a member of the either main or the Executive Board but he had an important post in the party and he was a deputy in the federal parliament.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I think that he was a deputy but that has nothing to do with it. What has an author have to do with any kind of lobby? A militant lobby at that. Is he maybe a criminal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I placed him in the party apparatus because he was a deputy in the Assembly and he was very close in the way he thought with all the of mentioned persons and it was horrible to read his articles and his comments. On one occasion he stated on television, I am quoting the following, "If it's necessary for Serbia, then it's okay to lie as well."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't understand the context of this Backa Palanka lobby. What does Brana Crncevic have anything to do with the Backa Palanka lobby?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he got an Audi 6 vehicle from Kertes. The term Backa Palanka lobby does not refer to people who are born there or live there but it refers to a group of people. The actual name Backa Palanka lobby comes from the fact that certain people happened to be from Backa Palanka. This is Pankov, Kertes, Jovica Stanisic who was from nearby, but the others were not too far from there, Vrbas, Kula, Crvenka.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Vucelic is from Crvenka. So probably on weekends he would go to visit his mother from Belgrade. He would stop by to have coffee at your Royal, which is in the centre of Novi Sad. Perhaps he did and perhaps he did not. I don't know that. But what is wrong in that or what is wrong in the fact that he said that the television is showing a patriotic programme?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I spoke here about circumstances, about people, about what certain people said in certain circumstances, and I don't believe that I am competent to evaluate what this has to do with anything else. If you feel that I should answer this question in a slightly modified way, perhaps then I will, but I'm not sure about the gist of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could you please tell me then in August 1992, you were talking about some kind of a meeting which they had. You said who was present. You said that Stanisic came and talked about the forthcoming London conference, and then there was discussion about what should be conjoined to Serbia and so on. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Do you know what the London conference was about? Do you know that it wasn't about any kind of territories but that these were political negotiations? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I'm aware of it. I know that the London conference, the main topic of it, was Bosnia and Herzegovina, but Croatia was also discussed because it was impossible to separate one war from the other war and one event from another.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The London conference dealt with the attempts to achieve peace. There was no discussion of any territories or any kind of changing of the compositions. These were political negotiations. Did you read newspapers at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But your objectives were the ones that I said you did. I heard this from the people that I talked about. I don't believe that I'm competent to reply to questions like this, but I will if the courts believe that I should. I talked about the facts that I had heard about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe that you are competent about that either, that is why I wonder that you're talking about these facts too. Do you know who headed the Yugoslav delegation at the London conference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is off the point and, Mr. Milosevic, you've got three minutes left if you have any other more relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Time goes very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You said that on that occasion, Stanisic said, and then you quote the same thing which you later wrote down in your alleged diary, that they should act subtly. Is that right? This is what you ascribed to him yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ascribe anything to anybody. I stated what people said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So he said also that activity had to be as subtle as possible. So on two different occasions, he and I used the same terminology and that is how you wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything strange in talking in the same manner about the same things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You talked about how Stanisic at a meeting conveyed a message of mine of some kind not to allow the Croats to come for All Saints Day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to step up security to prevent any possible surprises.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Do you know that the authorities of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem actually enabled, in cooperation with UNPROFOR at the time, for All Saints Day for citizens who did not live there to be able to come and visit the graves and that actually it was quite the opposite from the way you described it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. That is not correct. Perhaps for the period of 1996 and 1997, but in 1992 there was a clear marketing action or publication action on behalf of the Croat authorities to attempt a mass return to the occupied parts of the territory and people en masse came to those areas and then UNPROFOR had to turn them back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, UNPROFOR. They didn't let them pass because they were afraid that conflicts would inevitably break out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Very well. So let us clarify that UNPROFOR turned them back.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Well, we have some other questions. You said that Franko Simatovic was commander of the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
