utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: You said that Franko Simatovic was the deputy of Jovica Stanisic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the deputies.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay. One of the deputies. So there was nobody in between them. Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic were directly in coordination.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: So how do you explain your claim that Mihalj Kertes was the connection between the Red Berets and the service, i.e., between Frank Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic? How did now Franko Simatovic who was Stanisic's deputy and Jovica Stanisic be an intermediary like Mihalj Kertes relating to the Red Berets? Is this logical to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said anything like that, Your Honours. I would like to see the transcript where I said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: We have that in your statement, that he was the political connection of the Red Berets with the service. This is what you said. So he was an intermediary between Frenki Simatovic and Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this must be your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: When we're talking about the Red Berets, do you know that specifically that unit and its members carried out my arrest on the night of the 31st of March, 2001?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, do I need to answer this question about the arrest of Slobodan Milosevic on March 31, 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's relevant because he's talking about some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's only something he would have read in the papers anyway. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I should like to draw your attention to tab 3 of the evidence in connection with this witness, because I would like to ask some questions in that regard, based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were interviewed on three occasions by the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I can see from this with investigator Tore Soldal and Michael Stefanovic, you were interviewed three times: On the 16th of May, the 30th of May, and the 13th of June 2002; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the first occasion, just Mr. Tore Soldal was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that when you interviewed for the first time with these investigators, did you have your diary with you, the diary you kept over a number of years and that you also had the notes that you have presented here now, that you had both those things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I took my notes to that first interview, and they saw my diary on two occasions in my home when they were guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask to have possession of the diary? Why didn't they keep it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't ask me if they could keep the diary. Why not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you explain how you came to make these notes, the notes that are in evidence now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my statements and conversations to the investigators, I made use of my notes. I showed them the original of the diary and some newspaper articles that came out about me with different photographs. So they were able clearly to see what the notes were and what the diary was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you -- they didn't ask you for the diary or to photocopy the diary, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not feasible technically because I don't have a photocopy machine at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And they didn't ask you to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have the statements that you made to the investigators, and everything you say about the diary. This is all you say: "I kept a diary about all my affairs with the DB, the state security."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So is that the reason why you didn't hand the diary over to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Tapuskovic. The reason is that nobody asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to ask the Judges to look at page 10 of the English version and the BH version is 03276469.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: 6469 and 6470 are the last digits.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This makes up almost three pages, three written pages. On those three pages, that is to say the first page is in blue, marked in blue, and the whole of the next page is almost all in blue except for two sentences in red and then everything ends with a blue colour, blue markings again. Does that mean that on these three pages you write your recollections after ten years and that just that little portion, the little section was introduced and written on the basis of what it says in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't got these markings in colour as to what is at the original and what is not, but I can answer Mr. Tapuskovic's question. I didn't write anything after the passage of ten years, nor did I construe everything. Everything I say is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I just asked you about the passage marked in blue. You said when asked by the interviewers that you had jotted that down a few days before you left for the conversation with the investigators, whereas the red passage was extracted from the diary and copied out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that means three days before you came to see the investigators you wrote down everything that has been marked in blue, the passage marked in blue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote that passage down then. These were my concepts of what I wanted to say because I didn't want to leave anything out. Look at some sentences such as, "The intimidation of Marko [as interpreted] Popivoda," and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about one single sentence marked in red.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me which that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is on page 6470.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at this here. This is how it begins. "Petar Divljakovic told me in person that he was with the Red Berets, that they would create a Greater Serbia." That's what you write in the year 2001.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Tell me what line that is, what paragraph you're referring to. Page 6470.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The sentence begins with, "Petar Divljakovic," Divljakovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the 6470.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 6469. If Mr. Tapuskovic would turn back to that line, and it's 12 lines up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You gave me the wrong page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Witness. This is what you wrote in the year you did about the Greater Serbia. Now, the one sentence here, can you tell us how you worked? Why did you introduce this particular sentence in the place you put it in? And it says: "He said that several of them in Borovo Selo had killed Ustashas, Croatian police officers, and had them thrown into the Danube and soon after a comrade of his, Ivo Andric, got killed. I remember on one occasion he showed me his state security service ID card." That's the only portion that you introduce from your diary.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And all the rest you say when you wrote in 2002 that you wrote it in mid-1992. Why then did you not, when you extracted these things from your diary, why didn't you say when this was jotted down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this beginning with told -- he that rated as to how several of them, that passage? What are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What does it just say "mid-1992"? Why didn't you record the exact date if you had it recorded in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why there should be an a date. I just introduced this at different intervals. I said I didn't record the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right page 5 of the English version now, and it is 6455 in the B/C/S and it says during the summer of 1992. That's how the paragraph begins on page 5. And now everything is marked in red which means that you're copying out of the diary. There's just one sentence introduced here and you're writing this in the year 2002. "From the conversation, it was easy to deduce that Jovica Stanisic was the main personage among them and he was receiving instructions from Slobodan Milosevic which he himself often emphasised." How come you didn't write that in 1992? It took you up until 2002 to write that down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why should I? That was understood of its own accord. It's not a fact you could forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we come to page 6 of the English version, and this is marked all in red. There's just one single sentence marked in blue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please give me the B/C/S page number? I haven't got the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The last digits are 6458, I believe, and it is page 6 of the English version. Everything here is marked in red, which means it was copied out. Whereas in 2002, you say, "I was standing near the table to call the waiter if that particular gentleman happened to need anything, any food or drink, and I would tell the waiter what to bring and he would bring it without delay." Why are you writing this in 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could you give me the exact numbers of the B/C/S page? Otherwise, I'm going to think you're doing it intentionally, giving me the wrong page numbers. That's highly improper of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 7, in fact, and it's the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 57. You said 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not my intention to get you mixed up. Why did you write this sentence in 2001 which did not exist in your diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it because I expected a logical question from the inspectors. What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. You're getting ready for the questions you that might be asked of you because logical solutions and reasons would be sought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't think we would be talking about flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me this: On page -- on page 11 of the English version, next to the text there is an uninterrupted red line and a dotted blue line. What does that mean? What does that signify, the red line and the dotted blue line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give him the B/C/S reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: 6472 is the number.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That means that it is apart from the diary. A portion is from the diary and the rest of it is within my preparations for the interview conducted with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is your principle then? If you want to tell the true, then you should copy it out in full, integrally. So what is the criterion you're applying here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quotation by individuals attending the meeting, extracts from the diary and all the others. I don't remember all the things in the same way. Regardless of my high intelligence, I'm not intelligent enough to be able to remember everything from the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But it's the very delicate matters that you're discussing ten years later. Wouldn't you have had to rely on your diary more for those particular matters? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I explained all the circumstances surrounding my diary and why I didn't hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I now ask several questions in private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few matters arising from what you've just been asked. To clarify the position about your notes, the passages in red are those derived from your original notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see some passages which have quotation marks in them, other matters in summary form and so on. Derived or written out word-for-word, or a bit of each? Just help us so we can understand it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The quotations are verbatim from the diary, word-for-word, but when I copied it out I would use the perfect tense because I'm talking about events that took place in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you see, it's been suggested by the accused that -- I think that this meeting never happened, that he was never there, and that in reality you simply made all this up. If you look at what is the passage in your notes, pages 8 and the top of page 9 of the English version of tab 3 of the exhibit, and you can find it on -- I think it's page 6465. Just give me one minute. While I'm finding the right page for you, I can press on with the question. Apart from all the conversation that's recorded by you, it's also suggested that you must have completely made up things to the effect of the accused making comments about the position of keeping the Montenegrins under control unless they started to make troubles. Did you make details like that up or were those honestly recorded by you from what you heard? It's on page 6462 and onwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the details regarding this question which you have just put to me about the creation of an united Serbian state and with the help of Republika Srpska and the Republic of Srpska Krajina, the accused intends to keep Montenegro under control, is just as it was stated at the time. I am here in order to tell you about the facts and the information as I know them, and I would like to stress that in my conversations with the investigator and with the Prosecution, this is what I said because those people were only interested in the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said that there was some workers at the meeting who could confirm that the accused was there. You've dealt with, in answer to the accused, people who have either died since and one who is on the run and one who is awaiting retirement, but can you give us the names or identifications of any other people who it will be possible for us to perhaps pursue or even the accused to pursue through his associates to check on whether this meeting occurred? Can you think of any of the people who might be there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember some names. And as far as the names are concerned, perhaps it would be best to prove to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. You've been asked a little bit about why you should write down the notes of the meeting that you say you were at where the accused was present. Were you present in the room throughout the meeting and did you leave the meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present throughout the whole meeting except possibly when I needed to call the waiter in order to empty the ashtrays, change glasses, and this would last 20 seconds at the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what were your emotions about being present in a room where this accused, given the position he then had, was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must admit regardless of the fact that I did not agree with his convictions, it meant something to me to be in the same room as the president of the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that instrumental in your making notes of what was said the day or so or couple days afterwards that you did so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He asked you, did the accused, various questions about the activities of the DB, activities of which you were aware. You replied that they were connected to the government of which he was the leader. Was there ever, so far as you could judge from your contacts, any disapproval expressed apart from the incident with the gold watch, any disapproval expressed of the things that were being done coming from the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the question is not clear to me. Was I opposed to it or was it about my disapproval? The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My error. Did you ever receive any indication from those with whom you were communicating, your superiors at the DB, that what was being done was disapproved of by the government for which they were working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused asked you questions about the connection, if any, between him and criminals. You dealt with that, but the associated question is this: From your experience, was there or not connection between not individual criminals and the accused, but between politics and crime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a very strong and clear connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other matter of -- one other matter of detail and then I think I'm probably done. In the context of being challenged by the accused as to the accuracy of what you've said, he hasn't raised with you the accuracy of your identification of people at the Kula celebration of which you were shown a video. Do you remember now whether you were shown that video before or after you signed your statement that was provided to the office of the Tribunal -- the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it after I signed my statement in early July 2001. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a question by the accused about connecting Kertes to the Red Berets. I've been unable to trace precisely what the accused had in mind. It was towards the end of his cross-examination. The accused asked a number of questions about the witness's statement. I personally don't desire to put that statement in. It is of course available for you. There's one other matter of explanation that the Chamber might like and it's this: The accused quoted at some stage from a document that you don't have where the witness set out for the investigator how he had taken the notes from his original diary. If I can just explain. The document going to the accused last week that contained the notes contained part of a letter written by the witness to the investigator, part being excised for the same reason that one page of those notes has also been excised. The entire letter and of course the excised page is available for inspection by the Chamber should the Chamber want to see it for completeness and to be sure that the excised passage is properly excised. Alternatively, we can provide a redacted version of the letter that went to the accused containing the passage he read out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And apart from that, who has the original of this note?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The note was in the evidence unit. I unusually procured it to be here at court for the witness because the writing won't too clear. It's on the desk, I think, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is it a diary book you took note? I notice some times and telephones which look like a diary book. You took note on a diary book, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This note you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. In the diary, when I was going to the interview with the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you took notes from your diary on a separate diary book?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The agenda where I have my telephones -- where my telephone number is and everything, just by chance it's actually here with me in the witness room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there any special reason you used a telephone diary book to take notes from your diary? Is it that you tried -- you tried to make it look like the original diary? Is it your intention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I never said that was my original diary. What I said was during interviews I had after I left Serbia. So -- I'm speaking in this way so we wouldn't have to move into private session. The investigators asked me do I perhaps have the diary with me and I said what happened with the diary. And I also said that I would see whether the place where I'm residing now, if I had brought that other diary, that agenda book, with me. And then through the department, I sent these notes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I -- can I have the original notes, please, usher? And, Your Honour, I think it may be necessary for you to have a sight of if you're prepared to, on possibly an ex parte basis, the first sheet of these pages which -- in which case it won't be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not a complete book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be sufficient, I think, if you look at what we have, and you can see it's not a complete book. And of course -- I don't know what page numbers Your Honour had in mind, but the page numbers are page numbers stamped by the registry here when the documents are lodged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's a diary book. It's times and telephones, yes. It's torn some pages from the agenda book.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would appear so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That seems to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that is what the witness says. In fact, he says he has the book here with him, that particular book. I don't know if Your Honour has any more questions. I have one more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Something from the accused. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The one question is just to deal with the possibility raised by His Honour Judge Kwon about making these notes as if to resemble an original document. The Chamber will have in mind that the passages marked blue are broadly in plain speech but we can simply take one example on page 3 of 12. Right in the middle we can find that. I'm not sure we can find it. Towards the foot of page 6451, because it was a correction that the witness made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there's a paragraph, Witness C-048, that begins, "During in the 1990s, the service had a custom to enable its long time and approved collaborators." I don't know if you can find that passage easily and I don't want you to take time, but is that just an example of how you were certainly in the passages sidelined blue setting out a historical account of events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-048 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I set out a history -- a historical account of events, because in order to help the investigators, because these were people who were not so well informed about it. Not that they were not so well informed about it, but they were coming in from a different environment. So I just wished to explain to them the actual circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: A very unfair way of putting a question if I may say so. It was spoon-feeding the witness the answer, the context and everything. We would ask that the Trial Chamber make their own judgement about the matter which has been well covered in cross-examination and direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. I absolutely disagree with that. Limited time. Possibility raised by His Honour Judge Kwon. It's quite important that before the matter is lost from memory we can see the context and setting of this document and the witness has made it quite plain that the blue passages are indeed historic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, what was it you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one principled objection, Mr. May. Mr. Nice is using the term "original notes." This term cannot be used for a text written undoubtedly in 2002, because the diary does not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point as to how this came about, and we'll have to consider it in due course. Yes. Unless there are any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-048, that does conclude your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for inviting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until Thursday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- I don't think there's anyway we're going to be able to deal with it now. The Court indicated yesterday that might have some concerns about the protective measures of the next witness. Mr. Groome was going to be in a position to deal with that extensively -- not extensively, fully today. He now seems to have left. I can -- I think I can, in short, tell what you the position is, but I think we probably have no choice but to keep the witness here for Thursday and also have a back-up, because I suspect the Court is required for another hearing now, isn't it or this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We could have another five minutes. It may be best if the witness leaves, the arrangements having been made. We'll deal previously with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try and find Mr. Groome to deal with it in detail because he knows more about it than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can deal with it briefly. I think we know the broad point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that's all happening, can I simply use time because I wanted to say something about the list of witnesses that is attached to the application for time that you've received a week or so ago. That list is a document that I hope will be useful to you. I think it can actually be improved on. It's a document where there will be updates from time to time. I think it can be improved on in its present format in any event because I'd like to get at many names associated with witnesses rather than just letters because I think that's less helpful for the Chamber. I'll try and flesh out some of the details in the blocks of evidence to be given because again I think that would be helpful to the Chamber. But what I would like the accused to understand is that that document is not a list of witnesses in the order in which they're coming. The list being put together by topics in of course it's impossible to say of any witness he only speaks about Bosnia and MUP issues because probably he'll speak about something else as well. But the witnesses have been put together broadly by topics or by broad topics and the witness list will be the list that will be coming on a regular basis throughout every working week. However, the accused should understand, and I know he doesn't always have the time to read procedural matters in full, he should understand that the intention is that every bolded and underlined witness that there is given in that list is a witness who may be accelerated up and taken at an early stage so that if he or his associates have the time and opportunity to prepare in advance witnesses, they may want to focus on those bolded and underlined witnesses, they being witnesses whose importance and value is such that we will take them at an early stage if at all possible. So those are the only qualifications I wanted to make to the lists. And as I say, we will try -- the list of course will change over time as witnesses are called. The list may come with witnesses taken or excluded crossed out, but it's supposed to be a useful working document to guide the Chamber and the accused to what evidence is outstanding and also to what other evidence we think is important even if there's not going to be time to gather it. That's schedule three. Here is Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Dealing with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We had better be, I suppose, in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would ask that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The evidence of the next witness will be given in closed session, it being the position that protective orders - B-108 I'm told, thank you - protective orders were given -- protective measures, I should say, were ordered by another Trial Chamber, and Rule 75(F) and (G) preventing this Trial Chamber in any way interfering with those orders. We are bound by them. We think it right to hear the evidence rather than not, and accordingly, the order is made. No indication, of course, is to be taken from that as to any future orders about closed session. Help us --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The remaining witnesses for this week and next week are as indicated in the latest letter to the accused. There has, of course, been a slight change in the timetable because the last witness took a bit longer than was expected. If there are to be any changes following on from that as to next week's witnesses, we will send an appropriate letter immediately when we make that decision, but for the present, witnesses as ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the accused presumably can take it -- the accused can presumably take it that the order appears in the letters which you send weekly or so but that the general order may appear elsewhere in the way that you describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. It will always be in his interests, if he has spare capacity, to prepare the underlined and bolded witnesses on the list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
